Stiff Person Syndrome
Presentation of a Case With Repetitive Complex Discharges in Electromiograms
Pedro Enrique Jiménez Caballero, MD

Introduction: Stiff person syndrome is characterized by rigidity of axial and
proximal limb muscles, associated with muscle spasms, triggered by unexpected acoustic or somesthetic stimuli. It usually has an autoimmune basis,
in which the blood contains antiglutamate decarboxylase antibodies, and is
associated with different types of autoimmune diseases. The electromyogram
provides evidences of continuous muscular activity.
Case Report: A 41-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus type
I, Hashimoto thyroiditis, vitiligo, and pernicious anemia developed symptoms compatible with stiff person syndrome. In the electromyogram, in
addition to continuous muscular activity, there was evidence of complex
repetitive activity in the form of doublets and triplets.
Conclusions: Given the absence of clinical or electrophysiological neuropathic affectation, the presence of doublets and triplets in our patient could
be due to a subclinical functional alteration of alpha motoneurons. They
could produce the complex repetitive discharges when released from the
inhibition mediated by GABAergic neurons.
Key Words: stiff person syndrome, antiglutamate decarboxylase
antibodies, autoimmune diseases, complex repetitive discharges,
electromyogram
(The Neurologist 2009; 15: 227–229)
M

oersch and Woltman coined the term “stiff man syndrome” in
1956 to describe a series of 14 patients at the Mayo Clinic. 1
This syndrome is characterized by the insidious onset of stiffness of
the axial musculature which, over the course of years, spreads to the
proximal musculature of the lower limbs. Patients also present with
muscle spasms superimposed at the same location that are triggered
by acoustic or sensory stimuli or by passive or voluntary movements. The rigidity causes a lumbar hyperlordosis and gait to give an
appearance akin to a tin soldier. Cases of antibodies against the
glutamate decarboxylase enzyme is 60%, 2 for which reason an
autoimmune mechanism has been suggested. This hypothesis is
supported by evidence of the association with other autoimmune
diseases such as diabetes mellitus type I, Hashimoto thyroiditis,
pernicious anemia, myasthenia gravis, and vitiligo. 3–5 In other cases,
antiamphiphysin antibodies are found, and the syndrome has a
paraneoplastic nature, generally associated with breast or lung cancer. 6 The electromyogram (EMG) of these patients shows continuous activity of the motor unit with normal morphology, which is
especially prominent in paraspinal muscles and disappears during
sleep or upon administration of benzodiazepines. 7 The continuous
activity of the motor units is believed to be an alteration of the
GABAergic interneuronal inhibition through the spinal cord because
the glutamate decarboxylase enzyme synthesizes GABA from glutamate. 8

We describe a patient presenting with stiff person syndrome
associated with multiple autoimmune diseases and antiglutamate
decarboxylase antibodies. In the EMG, as well as continuous activity of the motor units, the patient presented with repetitive complex
discharges in the form of doublets and triplets. This is the first
reported case of this phenomenon. We attempt to explain the
physiopathologic basis of this neurophysiological observation.

The patient presented with repetitive complex
discharges in the form of doublets and triplets. This
is the first reported case of this phenomenon.

CASE REPORT
A 41-year-old woman had a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis
with secondary hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus type I, pernicious
anemia because of chronic atrophic gastritis, perioral vitiligo, and
extrinsic asthma.
The patient had symptoms that had evolved over 2 years,
consisting of lumbar pain and axial rigidity that hindered pelvic
waist movement with an associated lumbar hyperlordosis and typical rigid gait of the proximal lower limbs similar to a tin soldier. At
times, she suffered muscle spasms in the lower lumbar area triggered
by unexpected acoustic and somesthetic stimuli. The neurologic
examination of cortical functions, cranial nerves, strength, myotatic
reflexes, cutaneous plantar reflexes, and sensitivity showed no alterations.
Results of systematic blood tests of electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, creatine kinase, tumor markers, anti-Hu antibodies, K⫹ antichannel antibodies, and antiamphiphysin were normal. Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a dotted pattern at
1/320; anti-SSA, SSB, RNP, Jo-1, SCL-70, and anti-DNA were
normal. Parietal anticell antibodies were positive. Antiglutamate
decarboxylase antibodies were positive at 72. 23 UI/mL (normal
⬍1 UI/mL). Brain and spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging,
mammogram and thorax-abdominal CAT scand had no relevant
alterations.
Nerve conductions were within normal limits. EMG showed
continuous activity of motor units at lumbar paravertebral muscles
and iliopsoas. There was an absence of denervation. Repetitive
complex discharges were present in the form of doublets and triplets
at the anterior tibial muscle and tensor of fascia lata (Figs. 1, 2).
Study with surface electrodes reveled continuous muscular activity
in paravertebral muscles, abdominals, and the anterior side of the
thigh that did not disappear when relaxed and that increased considerably when experiencing unexpected acoustic stimuli. We delivered an intravenous infusion of 2 mg midazolam to control the
continuous activity of the left iliac muscle and confirmed that the
activity completely disappeared after 5 minutes. A dose of up to 300

mg Phenytoin per day was not associated with an improvement in
the doublets. Exteroceptive reflexes with right plantar stimulation
and recorded in vastus medialis and tibialis anterior of 2 sides, right
biceps femoris, and gastrocnemius lateralis were excessively enhanced with short transmission times. The latencies of the responses
were 130 and 70 milliseconds in the vastus medialis and tibialis
anterior on the right side, and 130 and 160 milliseconds on the left
side upon stimulation of the right leg. H wave showed an H/M ratio,
silent period, and recovery curve that were normal. Hyperventilation
and ischemia of the leg were not associated with changes in the
doublets.
We initiated treatment with baclofen in progressive doses up
to 25 mg every 8 hours and clonazepam up to 0. 5 mg every 8 hours
with clinical improvement of pain, stiffness and muscle spasms, and
gait. The EMG was repeated with the patient under this treatment,
and showed the disappearance of continuous muscle activity as well
as doublets and triplets. Coinciding with the death of her mother, the
patient presented an anxiety-depression syndrome accompanied by
increased axial rigidity and reappearance of more intense muscle
spasms. The EMG again showed doublets in the paravertebral
lumbar and psoas iliac. She responded to oral administration of 10
mg diazepam several times, until, after a few weeks, she returned to
her baseline state.

DISCUSSION
Our patient meets the clinical criteria proposed by Lorish in
1989. 1 These include stiffness in the axial musculature that slowly
spreads to the proximal musculature of the limbs, with superimposed
spasms caused by different stimuli, lumbar hyperlordosis, and absence of intellectual alterations and sensorimotor deficit, in conjunction with the evidence of continuous muscular activity in the EMG
that disappears after administration of Benzodiazepines. 9 –11 Some
authors divide this syndrome into 2 types: stiff trunk syndrome,
corresponding to the classic description, and stiff limb syndrome.
The latter refers to cases when the limbs was exclusively or predominantly affected. 12 Stiff limb syndrome usually develops with

relapses and remissions, can be associated with brainstem disorders,
may feature sphincter alterations, and features a weaker association
between antiglutamate decarboxylase antibodies and autoimmune
diseases. 13
The immunological basis of the syndrome is evident from the
association with multiple autoimmune diseases such as those represented by our patient: Hashimoto thyroiditis, pernicious anemia,
vitiligo, and diabetes mellitus type I. 14 The presence of nonorganspecific antibodies, such as antinuclear antibodies, is also common. 15 The glutamate decarboxylase enzyme is responsible for
synthesizing GABA, the neurotransmitter that is the main inhibitor
of spinal cord interneurons. The most widely accepted etiopathogenic hypothesis is a lack of balance between the catecholaminergic
and the GABAergic routes that control the activity of motor units,
giving rise to continuous muscular activity. 16 This hypothesis is
supported by the evidence of beneficial effects of drugs that favor
GABAergic neurotransmission, such as benzodiazepines, baclofen,
and even vigabatrin17 and levetiracetam. 18 GABA is known to act
by decreasing anxiety, and the effect of tranquilizers such as benzodiazepines is based on their reaction with the agonist of the
GABA-A receptor. For this reason, it is not surprising that patients
with stiff person syndrome suffer anxiety, and that this worsens the
spasms, as indeed seen in our patient.
Use of surface electrodes causes no pain and helps prevent
reflex spasms, allowing observation of continuous activity of motor
units at rest and recording of changes in this activity for long periods
while engaged in various activities. 19 In stiff person syndrome there
are no alterations of the peripheral nerves, for which reason nerve
conduction is normal. There is some indication of denervation, 19
although an atypical case has been reported with fasciculation,
pyramidal findings, and brainstem symptoms. 20
There are several diseases that are characterized by continuous muscular activity. Tetanus is distinguished by its clinical evolution and pathologic history. 21 Progressive encephalomyelitis with
stiffness is characterized by the appearance of cerebellum and
brainstem symptoms with atrophy at this level in the magnetic
resonance imaging, and the EMG indicates denervation. It is believed the symptoms are produced by alpha neuron hypertonia and
respond to treatment with benzodiazepines and baclofen. 22 Schwartz Jampel syndrome is hereditary, and appears in children after a
recessive autosomal pattern, chondrodystrophic changes, short stature and peculiar facies, and its EMG shows myotonia. 23 Isaac
syndrome, or neuromyotonia, is characterized by myokymia,
cramps, and fasciculations, in conjunction with muscle pain, hyperhidrosis, and atrophy of the hands and feet, with an EMG indicating
polyneuropathy with alteration of nerve conduction and postdischarges. It is an autoimmune process involving K⫹ antichannel
antibodies and it responds to carbamazepine and phenytoin. 24
The spontaneous action potentials of the motor unit discharging in groups of 2 or 3, or multiply, are known as doublets, triplets,
and multiplets, respectively. These potentials basically have the
same pathologic significance as fasciculation potentials, ie, they

represent spontaneous depolarization of a motor neuron or its axon
and are therefore usually observed in neuropathic conditions but are
also seen in hypocalcemia during tetany. 25 Our patient exhibited no
clinical or electrophysiological evidence of neuropathic dysfunction,
so the presence of doublets and triplets may have been due to a
subclinical functional alteration of the alpha motoneurons when
released from the inhibition mediated by GABAergic neurons. This
hypothesis is supported by the absence of response to phenytoin and
to hyperventilation or ischemia leading to the appearance doublets in
the EMG.
